chapter: Coming to New Orleans and building the band
title: Leaving for New Orleans and finding the band
summary: Left alone, he moves to the city, answers a letter about joining a band, finds his way by ferry, lodges with Rouchon and rehearses the new band.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: He never played with us because he left and went away, he went to Texas you see. He left and went to Texas. But Edmund, Robert, and Clowns, all of them we played together, we come up together you see, we played together you see. So well after that all left, well quite naturally that just left me. So now. I said well, I said it's my move now you know. So what I did Mr. Bill, I met up my mind and left. That's why I came here. I was down here living on Clio Street when this boy River, Elton, when he written on the country, a boy, his brother-in-law you see where his brother-in-law knows me. He said oh I know a fella you might get to play in your band. He told him, he said that fella called Thomas. He said oh you think he come? He said yeah you might come. So sure enough I was already down here you know. So I lived on Clio Street so the fella, I got the letter. He sent the letter out home and sent the letter back to me. So the boy explained me that I come up to go over the river you see. I had to get over on the ferry. So all I did I got the street cars like he said I went right on to the ferry you know. I got on the ferry. So he explained he said now listen, he said when you get off the ferry, if you want to ride the street car, you could ride a street car but it wouldn't be necessary because you could walk from there to Fred Street where he lived there you know. He lived in it by a message church and he told me, he said well, he said if you walk, you'll see a fire department. You know what I mean? Yeah. He said you come up to the fire department and you're tying. See, tying to your right and then when you get, when you leave the fire department right in the block they got a theater there. So he said you're tying and it comes like you're going to the woods. I did this like you say in the letter you know. So I went on and he went right straight to his house. So his wife said, told me, say, how you find, how you find out why we live that good? You, you do better if you wouldn't live here in the city. The first time I been in there all day is my life, Mr. Bill, I'm telling you. First time in my life, and I went right straight there. So, well the boy, this boy, he was working at the time, he was working for the railroad. So, well I went there at 12 o'clock, he was surprised you know, when he found me there you know. So, well, fine, well, he was talking, different things. So, I told him, I said, well I live on Kyle Street. He said, well, he asked me if I want to live with them. Well, I said, no. So, what I did, I went and live with the bass player, with Roushaw, Tiet Roushaw. I live with him. I stayed with him. I stayed on this side. So, finally, well, after that, this boy, Albert, Tom Albert's son. Oh yeah. He said, man, it would be better for you to come and live on the other side of the river, because we got all the bins on the other side, you know what I mean? See, of course, we got bins on both sides, but it would be over there, you know. You know what I'm scared of? I'm scared somebody's going to take me away from you see. Yeah. You see? Well, he's playing trambone too, you know, with Alton. So, well, I went on and I stayed. I stayed. I went over there and stayed with him. Yeah. I went over there and I stayed with him. So, finally, I moved. Up there, I moved from there and then I went and left. I got a room to myself. He said, a room. He said, a room. He said, a room. So, finally, well, then that boy, I got a wife, you see. Mm-hmm. So, all right. So, well, after that, we start, you know, the most thing we was doing when we first organized the band, we wasn't doing nothing but rehearsing, you see. We rehearsed three and four times a week, like on Sundays and everything. We could get jobs but we didn't want to take no jobs. Try and we'd get the band together, you know, everything straightened out. So, when everybody get out, nobody wouldn't have to tell nobody what to do, you see. Steve was playing trambone with us, too.
